subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: DNA replication copies the genome before cell division, ensuring each daughter cell inherits a complete set of genetic information. Errors can cause cancer, developmental disorders, or viral susceptibility.

sections.p: DNA replication is a semi‑conservative process that occurs during S‑phase of the cell cycle, producing two identical DNA molecules from one template.
b: Each new helix contains one original strand and one newly synthesized strand.
Replication is rapid (≈50 nucleotides/second in human cells) but highly accurate.

sections.p: Replication begins at origins of replication where helicase unwinds the double helix, creating replication forks. DNA polymerases synthesize new strands using the parental strands as templates.
b: Single‑strand binding proteins stabilize unwound DNA.
Primase lays down short RNA primers.
DNA polymerase δ (lagging) and ε (leading) extend DNA.
DNA ligase joins Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand.

t.b: Does the patient have a polymerase deficiency? Low activity suggests inherited disorders (e.g., polymerase γ deficiency) that can cause mitochondrial disease.
Is cellular proliferation increased? Elevated levels support rapid replication in malignancy; normal levels argue against high turnover.

sections.p: Replication is tightly controlled by cell‑cycle checkpoints and licensing factors to prevent re‑replication.
b: Cyclin‑E/CDK2 activates origin firing in late G1.
The G2/M checkpoint ensures replication completion before mitosis.
PCNA acts as a sliding clamp, increasing polymerase processivity.

sections.p: Faulty replication leads to mutations, chromosomal breaks, or incomplete genomes, underlying many cancers and genetic diseases.
b: Deficiency of folate or vitamin B12 impairs dTMP synthesis → uracil incorporation → strand breaks.
Mutations in DNA polymerase ε increase error rate → microsatellite instability cancers.
Herbal alkaloids (e.g., colchicine) can inhibit polymerases, causing bone‑marrow suppression.

sections.p: Understanding replication informs cancer therapy, antiviral drug design, and management of inherited replication disorders.
b: Antimetabolites (e.g., methotrexate) block thymidylate synthesis, targeting rapidly dividing tumor cells.
Nucleoside analogues (e.g., acyclovir) are preferentially incorporated by viral polymerases, sparing host DNA.
Patients with replication defects may present with developmental delay, anemia, or immunodeficiency.

t.b: If unavailable, treat empirically with folic acid and monitor response.
Is viral DNA replication active? High load guides antiviral choice; low/undetectable suggests treatment success.

sections.p: Key points often tested in exams.
b: Semi‑conservative model: each daughter DNA has one parental strand.
Origin of replication → helicase → leading vs lagging synthesis.

whenToSeekHelp: Unexplained progressive anemia with macrocytosis (possible folate/B12 deficiency).
Rapidly enlarging lymph nodes with constitutional symptoms (suspect replication‑driven malignancy).
Severe bone‑marrow failure after exposure to herbal toxins.

faq.q: Why is DNA replication called semi‑conservative?
faq.a: Each new DNA molecule retains one original strand, preserving half of the parental genetic information.

faq.q: What prevents re‑replication of DNA within one cell cycle?
faq.a: Licensing factors (Cdt1, Cdc6) are inactivated after origin firing and checkpoints block re‑initiation.

faq.q: How do antimetabolite drugs target replication?
faq.a: They inhibit enzymes needed for nucleotide synthesis, starving rapidly dividing cells of building blocks.

exam: Explain the steps of leading‑ and lagging‑strand synthesis and why they differ.
Describe how folate deficiency disrupts DNA replication and the clinical consequences.
Identify the cell‑cycle checkpoint that ensures replication is complete before mitosis.
